newsitem.title: UK: Hopes rise for N. Ireland talks after Blair paper.
newsitem.headline: Hopes rise for N. Ireland talks after Blair paper.

text.p: A leading nationalist politician said on Tuesday he was hopeful of a breakthrough in Northern Irish peace talks after new Anglo-Irish proposals due to be unveiled by British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Wednesday.

John Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), told reporters: "I think a real and historic opportunity now exists to take the gun out of Irish politics for ever and he (Blair) has clearly opened the door to lasting peace."

Hume was speaking after being briefed by Blair on the proposals designed to enable the Irish Republican Army (IRA) to call a ceasefire, allowing its political wing, Sinn Fein, to join stalled all-party talks on the province's future.
The key point of the proposals is "parallel decommissioning" -- peace talks jargon meaning the IRA would start to give up its huge cache of arms as the talks proceeded.

Under the previous Conservative government, defeated by Blair's Labour party in a May 1 election landslide, Britain insisted on a renewed IRA ceasefire and at least a start on the handover of weapons before Sinn Fein could join in talks.

But Blair hopes that by making lighter demands he can persuade the IRA to resume a ceasefire they abandoned in February of last year and commit themselves to political methods to work towards their goal of a united Ireland.

The IRA, backed by some Catholics, has waged guerrilla war since 1969 to end British rule in Northern Ireland and merge it with the Irish Republic. Northern Ireland's Protestant majority favours continued union with Britain.
Hume's reaction came after his political opponents, the leaders of the main pro-British unionist party in Northern Ireland, indicated they also might agree to the new proposals.
David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionists, Northern Ireland's main Protestant party, his deputy John Taylor and senior MP Ken Maginnis met Blair on Tuesday morning.

When he emerged from Blair's Downing Street office Trimble said parallel decommissioning was not his party's "first preference". But he said: "We indicated that we could go along...provided of course that that is what actually happened."
Neither Hume nor Trimble were shown the 12-page document which Blair has agreed with Irish Prime Minister John Bruton as the basis for a drive to get the talks moving.

Speaking on Irish radio, Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said he had also not seen it "When we do see them, Sinn Fein will study very carefully the proposals," he said. But Ian Paisley, leader of the smaller, hardline Democratic Unionist Party, accused London and Dublin of having "given in to the IRA" and said his party might quit the all-party talks.

The document was expected to be presented at peace talks on Tuesday. But Blair was forced to soothe feelings in Tuesday's talks with the Northern Irish party leaders after Bruton said in a television interview the proposals had been agreed.
Bruton, in New York with Blair on Monday for a United Nations environment summit, said the agreement would create conditions for rapid movement in the multi-party talks.
But Blair backtracked, saying: "I think it's possible that we have the basis of a way forward. But of course this has got to be agreed with all the other parties."

Blair, who is now due to unveil the proposals in a statement to parliament on Wednesday, said all possible clarification had now been provided to Sinn Fein, which now had to choose between the political path and violence.
The "troubles" in Northern Ireland careful represent one of the world's longest-running guerrilla conflicts, claiming the lives of more than 3,200 people over the last 28 years.
